en: In the *Buddha-bhāṣita-pātra-utsarga-sūtra*, Master Dao’an states that the translator was originally missing; it is now appended to the catalog of the Western Jin.
When the Buddha was at the Jetavana Vihāra in Śrāvastī, he was then with a multitude of bodhisattvas, beyond measure.

The Bhagavān was seated together with bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, the various heavenly kings, Śakra, Brahmā, as well as asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans; an incalculable multitude had all assembled and taken their seats.

The Buddha taught that for the sake of the Bodhisattva path, one undergoes diligent suffering through incalculable kalpas, enduring all the anxieties and labors of the hells, the realm of birds and beasts, and the hungry ghosts. Throughout the ten directions, one practices giving—gold, silver, rare treasures, carriages, horses, servants, as well as wife and children, head, eyes, flesh, and muscles—never begrudging anything as one bestows it upon the people of the ten directions through such diligent effort.

At that time, there were two hundred devaputras in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who, in their previous lives, had practiced the bodhisattva path but had not yet attained firm resolve. Hearing from the Buddha about the diligent and arduous pursuit of the Way, they all reflected that the Way was extremely difficult to attain; their minds then turned away from it and sought instead the paths of the arhat and the pratyekabuddha.

The Buddha, knowing that these sons of the gods intended to turn back, manifested a person of incomparable beauty and commanded him to take food of a hundred flavors to the Buddha’s location. The person knelt before the Buddha with palms joined in salutation and said to the Buddha:
“I pray that the Buddha will have compassion for me and accept this food.”
The Buddha then accepted it.
Among those seated in the assembly was a bodhisattva sitting before the Buddha named Mañjuśrī, who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“You should remember your past kindness.”
All the bodhisattvas in the assembly heard this and asked one another:
"Mañjuśrī! What kind of gracious favor did you bestow upon the Buddha in a previous life, that you now wish to receive the Buddha's meal?"

The Buddha then set his bowl down upon the ground; it immediately descended into the earth and traveled as far as the buddha-field of Rāvaṇa, a field named Pātala, where the bowl remained suspended in mid-air.
When the bodhisattvas in that land saw this, they rose, knelt before him, and addressed the Buddha:
“From where has this suspended bowl come? Why does it not fall to the ground?”
That Buddha said, "Wait but a moment;
you shall behold the majestic spiritual transformations of the Bodhisattva.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
“Go and seek out the bowl.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately entered eight thousand *samādhis* and traveled throughout eight thousand Buddha-fields, yet he could not see it. He then returned and informed the Buddha:
“I have searched for the bowl but do not know its location at all.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra,
“Go once more and seek it out.
Śāriputra entered ten thousand samādhis and traveled downward through ten thousand buddha-fields in search of the bowl, but he could not find it.
He immediately returned and reported to the Buddha, saying,
"I traveled downward through ten thousand buddha-fields in search of the bowl, but I could not see it at all.
The Buddha then commanded Mahākāśyapa to go and seek out the bowl.

Mahākāśyapa then entered twelve thousand samādhis and descended past twelve thousand buddha-fields in search of the bowl, but he could not find it; returning, he said to the Buddha, "I have searched for the bowl but did not see it at all."
Śāriputra addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
“Virtuous One, your lofty talent and merit are already perfected; your wisdom is fully complete, and you are the Buddha to come. You should know the whereabouts of the bowl.”
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Śāriputra:
"Although I am the one who shall next become a Buddha, with my merits fully perfected and my practices complete, I am not equal to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva."

For example, even if the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were filled with all manner of things—plants, trees, and grasses—as well as that many bodhisattvas, they would still be unable to know what the Buddha was contemplating within a single step.
“Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva knows profound samādhi; Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva alone is able to know the location of the Buddha’s bowl.
Śāriputra immediately rose, went before the Buddha, knelt with his hands joined in reverence, and said to the Buddha:
“I pray that you will have Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva go and seek out the bowl.”
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“Go and seek out the bowl and bring it here.
Mañjuśrī thought to himself:
"Śāriputra, you shall bring the bowl here without rising from your seat.

He then entered samādhi; just as when the sun rises its radiance shines everywhere, so too, for a bodhisattva who enters samādhi, there is nowhere throughout the ten directions that he does not reach.

Mañjuśrī reached his hand inside his *kāṣāya* robe and extended it past ten Buddha-fields. From each of the joints of his fingers, he emitted thousands of millions of rays of light; at the tip of each ray was a lotus flower, and upon each lotus sat a bodhisattva identical in appearance to Mañjuśrī. In the lands below, there were Buddhas, and upon the lotuses were bodhisattvas who all uttered the voice of Śākyamuni Buddha to pay their respects to those Buddhas, while simultaneously using the voice of Mañjuśrī to offer remote prostrations to them.
Just as with Mañjuśrī’s hand, it reached the buddha-field of Rāvaṇa; there, the bodhisattvas in that field addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is this hand? We cannot see its edge, nor can we see its limit."
The Buddha Rāṣṭrapāla said to the bodhisattvas:

"In an incalculable number of buddha-fields above, there is a field named Sahā. Its Buddha is named Śākyamuni. Seated before him is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, whose most honored radiance and wisdom are difficult to withstand; he has manifested such transformations as these."
The bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying,
"We now wish to behold together Śākyamuni Buddha and Mañjuśrī. Thereupon,
the Buddha Raivata immediately emitted from the crown of his head a thousand koṭis of light rays, which illuminated countless buddha-fields in the center and reached as far as the realm of Śākyamuni.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha, "Now there is this great fire emitting smoke, and in a mere moment the flames break out; is this the fire of the niraya hell?"
The Buddha said, "Do not speak such words. This is not the fire of hell; it is the fire within the Sahā world-system of the Śākya realm."
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha:
"Regarding this Sahāloka realm, for what reason is it named Sahāloka, and why does it have such fire?
The Buddha spoke to the bodhisattvas:
“Sahalodha-kṣetra is a land of mixed evils, characterized by the three poisons: lust, anger, and delusion.
The bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it appropriate for the bodhisattvas in the Sahāloka realm to practice patience and refrain from anger?
The Buddha said to the bodhisattvas:

"When people in the realm of Śākyamuni revile, insult, or beat a bodhisattva, that bodhisattva practices patience and never responds with anger; out of compassion for the people of the ten directions, they desire to deliver them, all of which is due to the empowerment of the bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual power and the grace of the bodhisattva’s patience. For this reason, it is named Sahāloka."
The bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Upon hearing this, we are greatly rejoiced that we shall not be born in the places of base people within the realm of Śākyamuni.
The Buddha Rāṣṭrapāla told the bodhisattvas:
"Do not speak such words; they cannot fathom the intentions of the bodhisattvas in the Sahālokadhātu world-system. The Buddha said, "I shall explain it for you all:

to the east there is a Buddha named Mūrdhaja, whose world-system is called Kāpila-madhyadeśa. The bodhisattvas in the Mūrdhaja Buddha-world fully accomplish the practice of the six pāramitās, yet this does not equal the practice of the six pāramitās by a single day and night of a bodhisattva in the Sahālokadhātu world-system, who brings to mind the sufferings of the ten directions and strives to deliver them all."

Why is this? In the Sahāloka realm, one undergoes diligent and arduous practice. It is like when a buddha-field is being destroyed and its world-system is consumed by fire; suppose a person wearing new clothes comes from the east and enters the fire, passing through it to the west, yet their body emerges unburnt—is that not difficult?
The bodhisattvas said:
"It is most difficult,
O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said:

“If a bodhisattva were to be reviled and treated with contempt for all that a bodhisattva in the Sahāloka world-system practices in a single day and night, that bodhisattva would practice patience and never give way to anger.”

For example, the difficulty faced by a person walking through fire without their body being burned does not even approach that of this bodhisattva, even by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, or a hundred-millionfold.
Twenty thousand bodhisattvas came forward before the Buddha and said:
"We wish to ascend to the Sahā world-system to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, as well as to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and the others."
The Buddha Rāṣṭrapāla said to the bodhisattvas:
"If you wish to go to the Sahāloka realm, first discipline your minds.
For example, just as the earth feels no joy upon receiving fragrant flowers or fine things, nor does it feel any anger when receiving excrement, urine, snot, saliva, pus, blood, or other impurities."
The Buddha said:
"For what reason do I speak these words to you?

Within the buddha-field of Śākyamuni Buddha, there are bodhisattvas who in previous lives made many offerings to various Buddhas; yet if a person has a quick temper, they may well intend good things but only teach them verbally with haste, which results in evil in this present life."
The bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The bodhisattvas of the Sahāloka realm have for a very long time in past lives made many offerings to various Buddhas while seeking the Way; by what cause and condition have they been born in this Sahāloka, a place of wicked and evil people?”
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:
"There are two causes and conditions for being born in this world in the Sahāloka realm:
first, in a previous life, they practiced together with Śākyamuni Buddha seeking Buddhahood; therefore, they have followed one another through successive lifetimes."
"Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, because the evil karma of their past lives has not been exhausted, are born in that degenerate age.
The bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha,
saying, "Now, by what causes and conditions do these bodhisattvas born in the Sahāloka realm manage to eliminate the evil of their past lives?"
The Buddha said:
"Good sons and good daughters who are born in the Sahāloka realm and seek the bodhisattva path may be born into poor households; by virtue of this, their evil karma from past lives is eliminated."
Furthermore, those who suffer from many illnesses shall have the evils of their past lives eliminated.

Moreover, those who encounter the sickness, emaciation, death, or the resulting grief and sorrow of parents, brothers, wives, or children shall, by this means, have the calamities of their past lives eliminated.

Furthermore, by encountering local officials, experiencing terror, abandoning one's parents, family, and property to flee in distress, and through such suffering, one may further eliminate the calamities and evils of past lives.
If one suddenly loses their wealth and property and falls into poverty and distress, by this means the calamities and evils of past lives are further eliminated.

If one is born in a wicked land where they are originally attacked and destroyed by another country, fleeing in flight with grief and anxiety, by this means the calamities and evils of past lives are further eliminated.

If one is born among the wicked and evil, being poor and lowly, with an ugly countenance, physically crippled, blind, or deaf—unable to keep pace with others—and if parents, brothers, wife, children, and kinsmen all hate them together, that person will suffer grief and anxiety; for this reason, they shall further eliminate the calamities and evils of their past lives.

If one hears of the existence of the good path and rejoices, seeking out an enlightened teacher to be instructed in the Way of the Sutras so as to open the mind and receive it from them, yet fails to find such a teacher and consequently falls into sorrow and anxiety—for this reason, the calamities and evils of past lives are further eliminated.

Furthermore, if one hears from afar that there is a teacher in a distant land who is highly enlightened, wise, and thoroughly realized, and desires to go there to receive his teachings, yet finds that the body is sickly and emaciated, the limbs are cramped and cannot be moved, funds are insufficient, and there is no companion with whom to travel—thus making it impossible to go—one will feel anxiety and sorrow; by virtue of this [repentance], one further eliminates the calamities and evils of past lives.

If there is someone who seeks out a good teacher and wishes to study and receive the scriptures from them, yet the teacher is greatly enlightened and thoroughly understands the essentials of the Way while the disciple is foolish, lacks wisdom, and their mind does not achieve understanding, they will consequently become sorrowful and anxious; for this reason, they further eliminate the calamities and evils of their past lives.

If there is a virtuous teacher who wishes to instruct a disciple in worldly matters and explain the Way of the Sūtras, yet the disciple is foolish and unable to practice forbearance, they may abandon the teacher and depart. Later, when they return to mind the teacher, the Dharma, and the precepts with great joy, their heart feels regret and sorrow; by means of this, they further eliminate the calamities and evils of their past lives.

If there are those who seek the Bodhisattva path, when they arise from sleep and see in a dream an enemy pursuing them with weapons, causing them fear and dread, their anxiety in that dream shall further eliminate the evils of their past lives.

If there are Bodhisattvas, followers of the Way, good men, or good women whose karmic retributions from past lives have not yet been exhausted and who would otherwise enter the hells after death to endure suffering for one kalpa, yet encounter a virtuous teacher who instructs them to repent for even one day and one night, then their headaches, fever, and all such ailments will be entirely eliminated, and they shall no longer enter the hells.

As soon as the Buddha Rāṣṭrapāla had finished speaking, Mañjuśrī reached down and took hold of the bowl; at that moment, the buddha-field of Rāṣṭrapāla, the countless buddha-fields in between, and all the way up to the buddha-field of Śākyamuni Buddha, were all violently shaken, causing all people to be struck with terror.
Śāriputra rose from his seat, knelt with his hands joined in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions has such a trembling occurred today, such that there is no one who is not struck with alarm and fear?"
The Buddha said to Śāriputra, “As for this earthquake that has occurred now, it is because Mañjuśrī reached into the bowl;
therefore, it has shaken. Śāriputra asked the Buddha:
"Where does the bowl reside?
The Buddha said, "The bowl is below, past countless buddha-fields. There is a buddha named Rāṣṭrapāla, and his field is named Padmaśa; the bowl resides therein."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Now these bodhisattvas, arhats, as well as devas, humans, asuras, spirits, and nāgas, wish to see the buddha-field of Rāvaṇa below, as well as the central buddha-fields, and they wish to see Mañjuśrī’s transformation in taking up the bowl."

Then the Buddha emitted ten billion rays of light from beneath his feet, which illuminated the countless Buddha-fields of the ten directions; thus, he saw everywhere the bodhisattvas in the Buddha-field of Rāviṣeṇa, and he saw Mañjuśrī manifesting transformations to take the bowl.
At that time, all the bodhisattvas, devas, humans, asuras, ghosts, spirits, and nāgas were filled with great joy;
yet all the arhats were overcome with profound grief and distress, shedding tears as they each said:
"If even a bodhisattva can manifest such transformations and perform such deeds, how much more so the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and radiant light, which are impossible to withstand?"
"We would rather enter the hells and emerge after a hundred kalpas, so that upon hearing the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas we might practice it; why should we worry about not attaining our vows?

Thus, the bodhisattvas from the buddha-field of Rāvaṇa, as well as incalculable numbers of bodhisattvas from the central buddha-fields, all came forth and arrived at the place where Śākyamuni Buddha was.
Each of the bodhisattvas thought to themselves:
"We shall go to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha to make offerings.

Among them, some bodhisattvas scattered flowers until they covered an entire buddha-field; some scattered incense; some scattered celestial robes; some scattered gold, silver, and precious jewels; and some produced the sounds of music. Within that single buddha-field, all these bodhisattvas came forward, placed their heads upon the ground in prostration to the Buddha, and having paid homage, withdrew to sit.

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva reached into the bowl and brought it out from among the seated assembly; all the bodhisattvas, arhats, devas, humans, asuras, ghosts, spirits, and nāgas were without exception filled with joy.
Śāriputra rose, stepped forward, knelt with his hands joined in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What kind of grace has Mañjuśrī bestowed upon the Buddha? For what reason does he now say that one should remember past kindness?"
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"In the past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Rādhanajī, who had sixty thousand bhikṣu arhats and seventy-two million bodhisattvas."
Among them was a bodhisattva named Janārdana. Rising in the morning, he entered the city for alms and returned with his bowl full.

As he walked along the street, a nurse carrying the son of an elder—the boy’s name was Vimalaprabha—saw the śramaṇa holding his bowl and set him down. The nurse took the child toward the śramaṇa, who gave him a honey cake. The child ate it and found it delicious; he then followed the śramaṇa away. The nurse pursued him to protect him, but when the child had finished eating everything, he looked back and intended to turn back.

The śramaṇa again took a cake and gave it to him; the boy ate the cake and followed the śramaṇa out of the city to where the Buddha was. Seeing that the Buddha was upright and handsome, with a body possessing the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, he could not look upon him enough; seeing the various bodhisattvas and bhikṣus, he rejoiced greatly.
The śramaṇa then instructed the child to wash his hands and rinse his mouth; he then took a bowl of cakes and gave them to the child, telling him to offer them to the Buddha:
"By doing so now, you shall attain peace and security, and later you will obtain its merit."

The boy took the bowl and the cakes, carried them before the Buddha, and with his own hand received the cakes and placed them into the Buddha’s bowl. He then passed them on to the assembly of Bodhisattvas and Bhikṣus, and they were all fully satisfied; yet the food remained as full as before, and the bowls remained as they were.
Having thus provided food for the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the community of bhikṣus for seven days, the young boy was greatly delighted and said to himself:

"If I offer one cake daily to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the community of bhikṣus for seven days until the offering period is complete, I shall surely obtain merit; by virtue of this single act of merit, may I attain Buddhahood."
The Buddha spoke to the bodhisattvas and arhats, saying:
"This was the kindness of that former time.
The bodhisattva Janārdana is none other than Mañjuśrī here now."
The young boy Vimalaprabha at that time was none other than myself.

That I have now attained Buddhahood, possessing the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and that I am endowed with majestic spiritual power and nobility to deliver all sentient beings throughout the ten directions—all this is due to the kindness of Mañjuśrī, who was originally my teacher.
All the countless Buddhas of the past were disciples of Mañjuśrī; those yet to come shall likewise be brought forth through the power and grace of his majestic spiritual authority.
"Just as children in the world have parents, Mañjuśrī is the parent within the Buddha-way.
When the Buddha preached this sutra, two hundred bodhisattvas in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven thought to themselves:
"The Buddha was originally taught by Mañjuśrī, who led us to cultivate merit and attain Buddhahood."
“Mañjuśrī, for what reason do you not attain Buddhahood while standing before the Buddha?
The Buddha said, “Mañjuśrī has deeply entered skillful means (*upāya*) to extensively transform sentient beings; therefore, he has not yet taken up the Way.”
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus:

“As for the two hundred devas and humans, and bodhisattvas, who previously intended to regret their pursuit of the two vehicles, having witnessed Mañjuśrī’s transformations and my response of gratitude, they have now all once again resolved upon the unsurpassed mind and cultivate the bodhisattva path; in future lives, they shall all become buddhas.”

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bodhisattvas, the community of bhikṣus, the devas, humans, asuras, ghosts and spirits, and nāgas were all greatly rejoiced; they rose and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Sūtra on the Setting Aside of the Alms Bowl Spoken by the Buddha
